title: Sepsis Prediction
answer: Sepsis prediction in intensive care and hospital wards uses machine learning to estimate the risk of sepsis onset or deterioration before clinical recognition. It covers adult, pediatric, and neonatal populations, and spans emergency department, general ward, and ICU settings. The goal is earlier detection than rule-based screening, using vital signs, labs, medications, and nursing notes. Scope includes model development, silent prospective evaluation, and integration into clinical workflows.

sections.body: Sepsis prediction in intensive care and hospital wards uses machine learning to estimate the risk of sepsis onset or deterioration before clinical recognition. It covers adult, pediatric, and neonatal populations, and spans emergency department, general ward, and ICU settings. The goal is earlier detection than rule-based screening, using vital signs, labs, medications, and nursing notes. Scope includes model development, silent prospective evaluation, and integration into clinical workflows.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Models typically run on hospital electronic health record systems, either as batch jobs on data warehouses or as real-time services consuming streaming vitals and lab feeds. Deployment requires HL7 or FHIR interfaces, identity matching, and low-latency inference for bedside alerts. Compute is usually modest, often CPU-based, but training may use GPU clusters on retrospective cohorts. Data storage and model registry sit within the health system's secure environment or a vendor cloud under a business associate agreement.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Work is done by extracting features from structured EHR data such as heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, white blood cell count, lactate, and antibiotic orders, sometimes adding free-text nursing notes. Models range from logistic regression and gradient-boosted trees to recurrent or transformer networks that learn temporal patterns. Training uses retrospective cohorts labeled by Sepsis-3 criteria or clinician adjudication, with careful handling of label delay and missing data. Evaluation emphasizes area under the receiver operating characteristic, alert rate, lead time, and calibration, often with silent prospective testing before live use.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Sepsis prediction models are regulated as medical devices in many jurisdictions, requiring validation, change control, and post-market surveillance. Hospitals must manage alert fatigue, clinician override behavior, and fairness across age, sex, race, and comorbidities. Liability questions are active, including product liability and wrongful death claims against AI vendors, and compliance pages track evolving FDA and EU rules. Data governance covers patient consent or waiver, de-identification, and audit trails for model versions and predictions.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward multimodal models that combine structured vitals, labs, imaging, and clinical notes, and toward continuous monitoring outside the ICU using wearable or bedside sensors. Federated learning and synthetic data aim to improve generalizability across hospitals without centralizing patient records. Prospective randomized trials and silent deployment studies are becoming the standard for evidence, while regulatory frameworks for adaptive algorithms are still maturing. Expect tighter integration with treatment guidance, but human review remains central.
